claims.text: Adding 2–5 wt% excess Ti and Zr getter powder will prevent alpha-HCP formation while permitting complete dehydrogenation without excessive oxygen pickup.
Ti and Zr act as sacrificial oxygen getters by forming stable TiO2 and ZrO2.
Ti and Zr oxides have more negative formation enthalpies than the corresponding oxides of Hf, Nb, and Ta.
Oxygen is released during decomposition of HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 below 900°C and can be scavenged by Ti/Zr.
The hydrides decompose in the sequence TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, then ZrH2.
The proposed hydride decomposition sequence follows from their formation enthalpies.
Heating at 5°C/min to 850°C will allow sequential hydride decomposition.
Holding at 1100°C for 30 minutes will ensure homogenization and getter activation.
Oxygen locally stabilizes alpha-HCP phases in this alloy system.
Rapid quenching suppresses the solute diffusion required for beta-BCC to decompose into alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC or alpha-HCP.
Water quenching from 1100°C will retain a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure.
The quenched material will contain no detectable alpha-HCP or alpha-Ti phase.
The resulting relative density will exceed 99.5%.
The resulting grain size will be less than 5 µm.
Getter use will produce fine TiO2/ZrO2 precipitates at grain boundaries.
The getter-derived oxide precipitates may strengthen grain boundaries similarly to TiO precipitates in NbMoTaWVTi.
Rapid solidification and oxide-particle pinning are responsible for the predicted fine grain size.
Sintering without sufficient getter leads to alpha-HCP formation and degraded mechanical properties because of oxygen contamination.
A quench rate below 100°C/s may permit decomposition into a dual-phase structure.
High yield strength will result from solid-solution strengthening and grain-boundary or precipitation strengthening associated with the fine oxide-containing microstructure.

contradictions.description: The prescribed regime quenches from 1100°C, whereas the in-situ experiment heats to and cools from 1200°C, so it does not directly test the stated thermal history.

The process is described as solid-state sintering and homogenization followed by quenching, but the fine-grain mechanism invokes rapid solidification without specifying any melting or solidification step.

The starting blend contains 2–5 wt% excess Ti/Zr, yet the final alloy is called equiatomic without explaining whether the excess getter is removed, fully converted into a separate oxide phase, or changes the matrix composition.
